entries.clue: People coming together for sports event (4,7)

blocks.note: a race is a people sharing descent, as in the human race
what people do when they come together at an arranged time and place

annotation.surface: A crowd assembling for a day's sport.
annotation.walkthrough: 'People' is the trap: it looks like the crowd going through the turnstiles and it wants the other sense, a people rather than the people. The two halves of the answer are separately ordinary words.
annotation.definitionFit: A race meeting is the day's card of horse races run at one course, one kind of sports event named by the sport it stages.

entries.clue: Dangerous game for which a routine result’s contrived (7,8)

indicatorNotes.contrived: Something contrived has been worked up out of whatever was to hand, so the letters in front are rebuilt rather than read as they stand.

blocks.note: fifteen letters of fodder, the S of 'result's' counted in as a letter

annotation.surface: A fixed contest in which the predictable outcome has been arranged in advance.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder fills the entry exactly, fifteen letters for fifteen squares, and the apostrophe-s is a letter rather than the verb the sentence needs. The game is said to be named for the tsarist officers who wagered on a revolver with one chamber loaded.
annotation.definitionFit: Russian roulette is the wager in which a player spins a revolver's cylinder and fires at his own head, which is as dangerous as a game gets.

entries.clue: Violent actions in university tackled by police officers (5)

indicatorNotes.tackled by: A player tackled by another is seized and held, so the letter in front is gripped inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: cops is the everyday word for police officers
u = university, the abbreviation used on forms and listings

annotation.surface: Trouble on a campus with police officers wading in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tackled by' sounds like the police doing the grabbing, and in the wordplay it is the university that gets grabbed — the single letter goes inside, not the other way round. Definition and surface both describe unrest, which smooths the join.
annotation.definitionFit: A coup is the forcible overthrow of a government, so coups are violent actions in the political sense: seizures of power rather than brawls.

entries.clue: Intervene and provide drugs to eliminate cold (7)

indicatorNotes.to eliminate: To eliminate a thing is to get rid of it altogether, so the letter named next is struck out of the word just found.

blocks.note: to medicate a patient is to dose them with drugs
c = cold, the letter on the tap, and it is the letter taken out

annotation.surface: Stepping in with medicine to see off a cold.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cold' looks like the ailment the drugs are for and is one letter lifted out of them. A doctor dosing a patient and a diplomat standing between two sides share nothing but these seven letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To mediate is to step between two sides and work at settling things, which is intervening in a quarrel rather than commenting on it.

entries.clue: Speak without stopping? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half defines the word as the railway uses it, an adjective for a service rather than a verb, which is what the question mark concedes.

blocks.note: to put a thought into words and let it out
the train or coach that runs through the small stations without pulling up

annotation.surface: Somebody talking on and on without pausing for breath.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface promises a person who never draws breath. The second half is a timetable word — the service that passes the intermediate stations — so the two senses are different parts of speech sharing one spelling.
annotation.definitionFit: To express a thought is to speak it; and an express train or coach is one that runs without stopping on its way.

entries.clue: Popular podcast finally wrapped up as planned (8)

indicatorNotes.finally: What comes finally comes at the very end, so only the closing letter of the word in front is taken.

blocks.note: what is in is what everybody wants this season
the letter podcast ends on
a meeting wrapped up has been brought to a close

annotation.surface: A popular podcast finishing its run exactly the way its makers meant it to.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Popular' means IN — fashionable, in vogue — and that two-letter reading is worth learning now, because setters use it constantly. The definition is the final word, though the sentence wants it as a comment on the wrapping up.
annotation.definitionFit: Something intended is what was planned: the intended consequence and the planned consequence are the same thing, both naming what was meant to happen.

entries.clue: Happy to have yummy apple (6,9)

blocks.note: a golden age or a golden mood is a happy one
yummy is the nursery word for it

annotation.surface: Being pleased to be handed a tasty piece of fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are everyday adjectives that happen to make up the name of a variety, so the enumeration is the only sign that a proper name is wanted. The variety is the pale yellow-green apple on every supermarket shelf.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Golden Delicious is one of the commonest eating apples sold in Britain, so 'apple' points at the variety by its kind.

entries.clue: Subtly funny nonsense? It may bring the house down! (3-3)

annotation.definition: It may bring the house down!
annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a sentence about the answer rather than a synonym for it, naming the thing by the one spectacular effect it has.

blocks.note: dry wit is delivered deadpan, quietly enough to miss
rot is what a person talks when they are talking rubbish

annotation.surface: A deadpan piece of drivel that has the audience falling apart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bring the house down' is the theatre's phrase for enormous laughter, and the fungus does it to the joists instead. Dry rot is the timber fungus that eats a British house from under its floorboards, and the exclamation mark is the setter enjoying the switch.
annotation.definitionFit: Dry rot crumbles the timbers holding a building up, so it literally brings the house down, while the phrase's comedy sense is the decoy.

entries.clue: Colleague eating an Indian cheese (6)

indicatorNotes.eating: Something eating another has it inside, so the two letters that follow go within the word just found.

blocks.note: your peers are the people you work alongside as equals
the article is taken exactly as printed

annotation.surface: A workmate tucking into a cheese from India.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Eating' is the hinge between the two readings: the colleague eats in the story and swallows two letters in the wordplay. The cheese is the firm white curd of north Indian cooking, the stuff cubed into saag and grilled on skewers.
annotation.definitionFit: Paneer is the fresh unmelting curd cheese of the Indian kitchen, so the definition names it by country and kind.

entries.clue: Transfer of secure bond ultimately made savings? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: Saving a life and making a saving are different things, and the question mark is the setter admitting that the surface's accountancy sense is not the one wanted.

indicatorNotes.Transfer of: A transfer moves things out of the place they were in, so these letters end up somewhere other than where they started.
indicatorNotes.ultimately: What is named ultimately is the last of it, so only the closing letter of the word in front is taken.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder
the letter bond ends on

annotation.surface: A safe bond moved between accounts and money put by in the end.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is financial, which is what hides a rescue inside it. 'Ultimately' reads as 'in the end' in that sentence and asks for a single letter in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: To rescue somebody is to save them, and the setter has swapped that verb for the accountant's phrase, which uses save in its other sense.

entries.clue: Bone from last bit of meat found in rice dish (7)

indicatorNotes.last bit of: The last bit of a word is the letter it ends on, and no more of it than that is wanted.
indicatorNotes.found in: What is found in a thing is sitting inside it, so that letter goes among the letters of the dish named next.

blocks.note: paella is the Spanish pan of saffron rice cooked with seafood or chicken
the letter meat ends on

annotation.surface: A bone turning up in the last mouthful of a rice dish.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a diner's complaint and the wordplay is one letter dropped into a Spanish pan. The answer is the kneecap, which sits over the knee joint and is the body's largest sesamoid bone.
annotation.definitionFit: The patella is the small disc of bone covering the knee joint, so 'Bone' names it by what it plainly is.

entries.clue: Restore control, say (9)

blocks.note: to rein a thing is to hold it in check, the way a rider holds a horse
to state a case is to say it

annotation.surface: An order to bring something back — order itself, for example.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like the setter's 'for example' hanging off the word in front of it, and it is a word in its own right meaning state. Three words is barely room for a definition and two pieces, which is what makes the seam hard to find.
annotation.definitionFit: To reinstate somebody is to put them back where they were — a sacked worker, a repealed rule — which is restoring them to their former standing.

entries.clue: Family member is somewhat keen, i.e. cerebral (5)

indicatorNotes.somewhat: Somewhat means to some extent and not the whole of it, so a part of what follows is wanted — a run of letters taken as they lie.

blocks.note: five letters in an unbroken run, beginning inside the first word and carrying on across the punctuation

annotation.surface: Somebody who is fairly sharp and fairly intellectual with it.
annotation.walkthrough: The abbreviation planted in the middle is what makes the run so hard to see: full stops and commas are invisible to the letters, and the eye stops at them anyway.
annotation.definitionFit: A niece is the daughter of your brother or sister, so she is a family member named by her exact relation to you.

entries.clue: Intro to theme with a certain musical sound (4)

indicatorNotes.Intro to: An intro is what comes at the front, so only the opening letter of the word after it is taken.

blocks.note: the letter theme opens with
a certain person means one particular person

annotation.surface: The opening of a theme tune with a particular sound to it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A certain' is the phrase to store away: a certain somebody is one somebody, three letters for two words. The theme and the sound keep the whole sentence inside a single recording studio.
annotation.definitionFit: A tone is a sound of definite pitch, the steady note a tuning fork gives out, so the definition names it by kind.

entries.clue: Nerds were upset about a current affairs host (10)

indicatorNotes.upset: Something upset has been knocked over and its contents spilled, so the letters will not stay in the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.about: What is about a thing is all round it, so the letters just re-set close around the one that follows.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder
the article taken as a single letter, and set inside those nine

annotation.surface: Geeks in a huff over a television presenter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' is doing real work: the shuffled letters have to close round the A rather than simply run alongside it. 'Upset' reads as the geeks' mood and is the instruction that scrambles them.
annotation.definitionFit: A newsreader is the presenter who fronts a television bulletin, which is what hosting the current affairs of the day amounts to.

entries.clue: Small indication of sadness? (8)

blocks.note: read as a faint hint that something is wrong, and meant as a measure of liquid — a drop is as small as liquid comes
read as what the hint is about, and meant as the grief that squeezes the liquid out of the eye

annotation.surface: The faintest sign that somebody is unhappy.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing here comes apart into letters. The clue turns on 'small' switching from the size of a hint to the size of a bead of water, and the question mark is the only warning that the sentence has two jobs.
annotation.definitionFit: A teardrop is the single bead of water that runs from a crying eye, so the definition describes it by size and by cause at once.

entries.clue: Honest shareholders’ position? (5,5)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half is not a synonym but a picture, placing the shareholders where the phrase's own words put them, over the board of directors — which is what the question mark flags.

blocks.note: open and straight in one's dealings, with nothing kept back
the owners of a company rank over the directors who sit on its board

annotation.surface: The stance taken by a company's straight-dealing shareholders.
annotation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from the card table, where a player keeping his hands above the board cannot deal off the bottom of the pack. Read the second half literally and the shareholders are simply sitting higher than the directors.
annotation.definitionFit: Above board means open and honest, from the gambler whose hands stay in sight; and in a company the shareholders stand above the board, which is the second reading.

entries.clue: In the centre of dam, it’s turbulent (6)

indicatorNotes.turbulent: Turbulent water churns and is never twice the same, so the letters in front of the word come out in another order.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, the apostrophe-s counted in as a letter

annotation.surface: Water at a dam boiling up in the middle of it.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the opening phrase, which reads as part of the description of the dam — that is the whole disguise. The apostrophe-s is a letter here, not the verb the sentence appears to need.
annotation.definitionFit: Amidst is the older, more literary form of amid: to stand amidst the trees is to have them all round you, in the thick of them.

entries.clue: Burden of work supported by journalists (7)

indicatorNotes.supported by: What supports a thing stands underneath it, and in a down entry underneath means further on, so these letters come second.

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a composer's work, and it is numbered on every concert programme
the press is the newspapers and the reporters who fill them

annotation.surface: A workload carried on the shoulders of the newspapers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Burden' is a verb here, not the noun the surface wants — the sentence offers a load of work and the definition wants what you do to people. 'Supported by' is the only thing saying which piece goes underneath.
annotation.definitionFit: To oppress people is to weigh them down with something they cannot shift, which is burdening them when the load is authority rather than cargo.

entries.clue: One not sugarcoating facts about Hollywood elite (7)

blocks.note: re = about, the word at the head of a memo
the A-list is the top rank of film stars, the names that open a picture

annotation.surface: Somebody telling the blunt truth about the biggest film stars.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like the preposition joining the truth-teller to the stars, and it is the answer's first two letters. The A-list is the film industry's own term for its most bankable people.
annotation.definitionFit: A realist takes things as they are rather than as one would wish them, so nothing gets sweetened in the telling.

entries.clue: Knocking back lager is a mistake (4)

indicatorNotes.Knocking back: To knock a drink back is to send it down the way it came, and in an across entry that means the letters are read from right to left.

blocks.note: Pils is the pale lager sold in every British pub, and its four letters are set down from the back

annotation.surface: Downing a pint of lager, which turns out to be a bad idea.
annotation.walkthrough: Pils is short for Pilsner, the pale Czech style most British lager copies. 'Knocking back' does the drinker's job and the grid's at the same time, which is what makes the sentence read so naturally.
annotation.definitionFit: A slip is a small mistake made by accident rather than ignorance: a slip of the tongue, a slip of the pen.

entries.clue: Refinement of European language (6)

blocks.note: the last smoothing that turns roughness into good manners
the Slavic tongue spoken in Warsaw, whose name takes a capital letter

annotation.surface: The elegance of a language spoken somewhere in Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: The trick is a capital letter the printed clue cannot show: one sense needs a big P and the other a small one, and the two are said differently as well. 'Of' welds them into a single phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Polish is the sheen rubbing gives a surface, and so the refinement of a person's manner; capitalised, it is the language of Poland.

entries.clue: Individual doing little except relaxing, primarily? (5)

annotation.definition: Individual doing little except relaxing, primarily

indicatorNotes.primarily: Primarily points at what comes first, so each word of the list gives up only the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: five words in the order printed, each handing over its opening letter

annotation.surface: A person whose day amounts to very little beyond taking it easy.
annotation.walkthrough: The sentence describes the man and spells him at the same time, so there is no separate definition to hunt for. 'Primarily' reads as 'mostly' in the description and as an instruction in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is what the word means: somebody who does next to nothing and spends the day at rest.

entries.clue: Sensible thing kids often do in science class (9)

annotation.definition2: thing kids often do in science class

blocks.note: down to earth, good at getting things done rather than theorising about them

blocks.clueFragment: thing kids often do in science class
blocks.note: the British school lesson spent at the bench with the bunsen burners instead of taking notes

annotation.surface: A sensible activity for children in a science lesson.
annotation.walkthrough: The two halves are different parts of speech: the first an adjective, the second a noun. In British schools that noun is the hands-on lesson, the one where pupils do an experiment and write it up afterwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Practical means level-headed and useful in the real world, which is what calling somebody sensible says; and a practical is the experiment session British pupils sit in science.

entries.clue: Dance team no good on regular occasions (5)

indicatorNotes.on regular occasions: Something done on regular occasions happens at an even spacing, so the letters are picked at a fixed step — every other one.

blocks.note: every other letter of the three words read as one continuous run, starting with the first

annotation.surface: A dance troupe that is no use much of the time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'No good' is the trap: it is the crossword's usual NG, and here it is only letters to be counted through. The dance came out of the bars of Buenos Aires before Paris took it up.
annotation.definitionFit: The tango is the close-held Argentine ballroom dance of sudden turns and abrupt pauses, so 'Dance' names it by its kind.

entries.clue: Release from group costing nothing (3,4)

blocks.note: a set is a group of things taken together: a set of tools, a set of friends
what costs nothing is had for nothing

annotation.surface: Getting out of a club that charges no membership fee.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Release from' reads as a single phrase, which is the trap: the definition stops at the first word and 'from' is only the join. A set can be a group of people as readily as a group of things.
annotation.definitionFit: To set free is to let go — a prisoner, a caught bird — which is releasing them in the plainest sense of the verb.

entries.clue: Fiery genius somehow capturing supporter’s heart (7)

indicatorNotes.somehow: Doing a thing one way or another leaves the manner of it open, so the letters in front need not stay as they were given.
indicatorNotes.capturing: To capture a thing is to take it and hold on to it, so the letters just re-set close around the one that follows.
indicatorNotes.heart: The heart of a word is the letter at its very middle, with as many letters on one side of it as the other.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder
the middle letter of supporter, with four letters standing either side of it

annotation.surface: A brilliant talent winning the heart of a devoted fan.
annotation.walkthrough: The heart wanted is not the fan's affection but the letter at the centre of the word 'supporter'. Igneous rocks — granite, basalt, pumice — are the ones that cooled out of molten magma.
annotation.definitionFit: Igneous means of fire, from the Latin ignis: igneous rock is what molten magma hardens into, so 'Fiery' is the word's literal sense.

entries.clue: Descriptions of old jobs (11)

blocks.note: ex- is the prefix for the former holder of a thing: an ex-wife, an ex-president
a position is a post somebody holds at work

annotation.surface: Accounts of the work somebody used to do.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old jobs' splits into a prefix and the word it would normally be hyphenated onto, and 'of' is doing nothing but joining. An exposition is a setting-out of an argument as well as a trade fair.
annotation.definitionFit: An exposition is a full setting-out of a subject — the passage that explains how things stand — which is description at length rather than in passing.
